A household or business in Sweden (and in many other countries) needs two separate agreements to have power delivered and billed: a grid (network) contract and an electricity supply contract. Here’s how they differ:

1. Parties Involved  
   • Grid contract: You sign with your regional network operator (nätägaren). This is the company that owns and maintains the local power lines, transformers and meters.  
   • Electricity supply contract: You sign with an electricity retailer or supplier (elhandelsbolag). This is the company that actually sells you the kilowatt-hours.

2. What You’re Paying For  
   • Grid contract: Covers the cost of transporting electricity to your property, maintaining the grid infrastructure, and metering. Charges are largely fixed or capacity-based (monthly fees plus a small per-kWh network usage fee). These fees are regulated by the Swedish Energy Markets Inspectorate (Ei).  
   • Electricity supply contract: Covers the commodity price of the electricity itself

Control and regulation technology (often called “control systems” or “automation technology”) is the branch of engineering and applied science concerned with monitoring, managing and optimizing physical processes. In practice it consists of four main components:  
1. Sensors and measurement devices  
   – Gather real-time data on key variables (for example temperature, pressure, flow rate, humidity, CO₂ levels).  
2. Controllers (hardware and software)  
   – Compare measured values against desired set-points and calculate corrective actions.  
   – Often implement control algorithms (PID control, on/off control, predictive control, etc.).  
3. Actuators and final elements  
   – Translate controller outputs into physical actions (e.g. by opening/closing valves, adjusting dampers, switching pumps or fans on/off, dimming lights).  
4. Communication and visualization  
   – Link all devices via wired or wireless networks (fieldbus, Modbus, BACnet, KNX, OPC, etc.).

Expanding an existing building control system typically involves both hardware and software additions, careful integration planning, and commissioning. Below is a step-by-step approach:

1. Assess the Current System  
   • Inventory your existing controllers, I/O modules, field devices (sensors, actuators, valves, dampers) and communication network (e.g. BACnet, Modbus, KNX).  
   • Identify capacity limits – available I/O points on PLCs or building-automation controllers, network bandwidth, and software licensing.

2. Define the Expansion Scope  
   • New zones or functions (e.g. HVAC zones, lighting control, shading, metering).  
   • Performance targets (energy savings, improved comfort, fault detection).  
   • Certification or compliance requirements (e.g. upgrades to meet a higher EPC energy class).

3. Select and Size Additional Hardware  
   • I/O Expansion Modules – match the existing controller family or choose decentralised I/O racks if you prefer a distributed architecture.

In the EV-charging industry the informal “break” between normal (or standard) charging and fast charging is generally set around the 22 kW level for AC chargers, with DC chargers stepping in at higher power levels. A more detailed breakdown looks like this:

1. Slow/“trickle” charging  
   • Single-phase AC, up to about 3.7 kW (household outlets or Schuko/Type 2 on 10 – 16 A)  
   • Adds roughly 10–15 km of range per hour

2. Standard/“normal” charging  
   • Single- or three-phase AC, typically up to 7.4 kW (32 A single-phase) or 11–22 kW (16–32 A three-phase)  
   • Adds 20–50 km of range per hour

3. Fast/“rapid” charging  
   • Usually DC, starting at about 25–50 kW and up (some AC wallboxes go to 43 kW or even 50 kW three-phase, but once you exceed 22 kW AC most operators term it “accelerated” rather than standard)  
   • At 50 kW DC you can expect roughly 150–200 km of range in 30 minutes; ultra-fast stations push 100 kW, 150 kW or more

Load balancing for EV charging is a smart‐charging strategy that dynamically allocates the available electrical power among one or more chargers to

 • Prevent overloads on local circuits or the public grid  
 • Make full use of the maximum capacity you have (for example on a single‐phase or three‐phase supply)  
 • Reduce peak‐demand charges and energy costs  
 • Improve overall grid stability by smoothing out spikes in consumption  

How it works  
1. Measurement & monitoring  
   – Each charging point (or a central controller) continuously monitors real‐time power draw, the total supply capacity of the feeder (or transformer), and sometimes even upstream grid constraints.  
2. Decision logic  
   – A local controller or a cloud-based energy management system compares current demand to available capacity.  
   – If demand exceeds the set limit, the system throttles back charging power at one or more stations. Conversely, if spare capacity is available, it can increase charge rates.

In Sweden (and under most European lighting‐design standards such as SS-EN 12464-1), stairwells should be illuminated to achieve a maintained horizontal illuminance of at least 100 lux on the walking surface (steps and landings). Key points:

• Recommended level:  
  – 100 lux average on treads and landings for normal use.  
  – In higher‐risk or public buildings you may design for 150–200 lux.  
• Uniformity (minimum/average):  
  – Uo ≥ 0.4 (i.e. the minimum point should not fall below 40 % of the average illuminance).  
• Measurement height:  
  – Typically at 0.85 m above the step nosing or floor slab.  
• Colour and quality:  
  – Colour temperature 3 000–4 000 K, colour rendering index (CRI) ≥ 80.  
• Emergency lighting:  
  – Even in the event of a power failure, a minimum of 1–5 lux (depending on national regulations) must be maintained along escape routes.

In Sweden stairwells are normally regarded as “unoccupied” but frost-protected zones and in Boverket’s Building Regulations (BBR) they belong to heating‐category H4. That category requires a design temperature of

    12 °C ± 2 °C

(so in practice you keep the stairwell between about 10 °C and 14 °C).  

Keeping the temperature at this level will

• prevent frost damage and pipe‐burst risk  
• avoid persistent condensation and mould growth  
• ensure a safe, non-slippery environment for users  

If you only need minimal frost protection (and have no water installations in the enclosure), some designers accept down to 8 °C, but the generally recommended set-point in common residential stairwells is 12 °C.

Ventilation balancing is the process of measuring, adjusting and commissioning a mechanical ventilation system so that its supply and exhaust airflows match the design intentions. When done correctly, balancing ensures that each room receives exactly the right amount of fresh air, and that stale or humid air is removed at the intended rate. 

How proper ventilation balancing affects energy use  
1. Reduces over-ventilation losses  
   – Unbalanced systems often deliver too much supply air (or too little exhaust), causing excess heat or cooling to be exhausted outdoors.  
   – By matching the actual airflow to the design airflow, you avoid wasting heating or cooling energy on air you don’t really need.  

2. Improves heat-recovery performance  
   – Many balanced ventilation systems include a heat-recovery unit (mechanical heat recovery ventilator, HRV, or energy-recovery ventilator, ERV).  
   – When supply and exhaust flows are equal, the heat exchanger operates at its optimal airflow
